claim: The human genome contains approximately 500 eukaryotic protein kinases.
source: The human genome contains approximately 500 eukaryotic protein kinases which coordinate signaling networks in cells by catalyzing the transfer of a phosphate group from ATP to serine, threonine, or tyrosine residues (Manning, 1995; Modi and Dunbrack, 2019a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Manning, 1995 and Modi and Dunbrack, 2019a

claim: The GO database identifies 351 (~70%) of protein kinases as serine/threonine kinases (STKs).
source: The GO (gene ontology) database identifies 351 (~70%) of these enzymes as serine/threonine kinases (STKs) and 90 (~18%) as tyrosine kinases (TKs).
evidence: Supported by reference to the GO database

claim: The GO database identifies 90 (~18%) of protein kinases as tyrosine kinases (TKs).
source: The GO (gene ontology) database identifies 351 (~70%) of these enzymes as serine/threonine kinases (STKs) and 90 (~18%) as tyrosine kinases (TKs).
evidence: Supported by reference to the GO database

claim: STKs are an ancient class of protein kinases that predate the divergence of the three domains of life (bacteria, archaea, eukaryote).
source: STKs are an ancient class of protein kinases that predate the divergence of the three domains of life (bacteria, archaea, eukaryote) (Stancik et al., 2018), whereas TKs are a more recent evolutionary innovation, having diverged from STKs about 600 million years ago during early metazoan evolution (Miller, 2012; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stancik et al., 2018

claim: TKs diverged from STKs about 600 million years ago during early metazoan evolution.
source: STKs are an ancient class of protein kinases that predate the divergence of the three domains of life (bacteria, archaea, eukaryote) (Stancik et al., 2018), whereas TKs are a more recent evolutionary innovation, having diverged from STKs about 600 million years ago during early metazoan evolution (Miller, 2012; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Miller, 2012 and Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2016

claim: Type-II inhibitors only bind when the kinase adopts an inactive 'DFG-out' conformation.
source: A particular class of ATP-competitive kinase inhibitors which were proposed to have a high potential for selectivity are called 'type-II inhibitors' which only bind when the kinase adopts an inactive 'DFG-out' conformation.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text

claim: The activation loop is approximately 20 residues long.
source: 'DFG' (Asp-Phe-Gly) refers to a conserved catalytic motif located at the N-terminus of an ~20 residue-long 'activation loop' that is highly flexible and controls the activation state of the kinase and the structure of the substrate binding surface.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text

claim: Dunbrack and co-workers identified eight major conformational states in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) based on DFG motif metrics.
source: Recently, Dunbrack and co-workers identified eight major conformational states in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) based on these metrics (Modi and Dunbrack, 2019b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Modi and Dunbrack, 2019b

claim: The activation loop undergoes a ~17 Å reorganization when transitioning from the active 'extended' conformation to the classical DFG-out 'folded' conformation.
source: We refer to these states of the activation loop collectively as 'folded', to describe its ~17 Å reorganization relative to the active 'extended' conformation, wherein the substrate binding surface has been 'folded up' toward the kinase N-terminal lobe and away from the αC-helix.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text

claim: Type-II inhibitors have a long chemical fragment that allows them to bind across the gatekeeper and form interactions with residues in the back pocket.
source: Type-II inhibitors typically have a long chemical fragment that allows them to bind across the gatekeeper and form interactions with residues in the back pocket.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text

claim: Type-I inhibitors can bind to either DFG-in or DFG-out conformations.
source: In contrast, type-I inhibitors (the majority of kinase drugs) occupy the ATP pocket but not the back pocket and can bind to either DFG-in or DFG-out.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text

claim: Different kinase sequences have different propensities to adopt DFG-out in the absence of inhibitor.
source: For these reasons, it has been proposed that type-II inhibition holds greater potential for the design of highly selective drugs (Vijayan et al., 2015; Davis et al., 2011; Anastassiadis et al., 2011); it has been shown that different kinase sequences have different propensities to adopt DFG-out in the absence of inhibitor (Haldane et al., 2016; Hari et al., 2013), and the DFG-out back pocket has been suggested to have a lesser degree of sequence and structural homology between kinases (Liu and Gray, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haldane et al., 2016 and Hari et al., 2013

claim: STKs have an unfavorable contribution to the binding of type-II inhibitors relative to TKs.
source: Analysis of the type-II hit rate distributions for STKs and TKs from the Davis assay (Figure 1A) indicates that STKs, on average, have an unfavorable contribution to the binding of type-II inhibitors relative to TKs.
evidence: Based on analysis of experimental binding assay data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Gatekeeper size has an important influence on type-II binding for both STKs and TKs.
source: By plotting the hit rate distributions for STKs and TKs where the gatekeeper is either small or large (Figure 1A) we confirm that gatekeeper size has an important influence on type-II binding for both STKs and TKs (Azam et al., 2008).
evidence: Confirmed by data in Figure 1A and supported by citation to Azam et al., 2008

claim: TKs tend to have small gatekeepers in comparison to STKs.
source: Because TKs tend to have small gatekeepers in comparison to STKs (Zuccotto et al., 2010; Taylor and Kornev, 2011), we considered this as a possible explanation behind the bias for TKs to have larger type-II hit rates.
evidence: Supported by citations to Zuccotto et al., 2010 and Taylor and Kornev, 2011

claim: Recent solution NMR experiments with Abl kinase revealed two DFG-out conformational states.
source: Recent solution NMR experiments with Abl kinase revealed two DFG-out conformational states (Xie et al., 2020) one where the DFG motif has flipped 'DFG-in to DFG-out' but the activation loop remains in a 'minimally perturbed' active-like conformation, and the other state is a classical 'folded' DFG-out conformation where the activation loop has moved ~17 Å away from the active conformation (Figure 1B), and the DFG motif is in a 'classical DFG-out' (Vijayan et al., 2015) or 'BBAminus' (Modi and Dunbrack, 2019b) state.
evidence: Supported by citation to Xie et al., 2020 and shown in Figure 1B

claim: Type-II inhibitors preferentially bind to the folded DFG-out state.
source: Type-II inhibitors were shown to preferentially bind to this folded DFG-out state, confirming observations that Abl is almost always co-crystallized with type-II inhibitors in this conformation.
evidence: Based on observations from NMR experiments and crystallographic data

claim: BIRB-796 binds to MAPK14 about 7 kcal/mol more strongly than imatinib.
source: For example, BIRB-796 (Pargellis et al., 2002) binds to MAPK14 about 7 kcal/mol more strongly than imatinib.
evidence: Based on comparison of binding affinities, with citation to Pargellis et al., 2002

claim: TKs have, on average, weaker N-terminal anchor, RD-pocket, and C-terminal anchor interactions than STKs.
source: In summary, TKs are suggested by the Potts statistical energy model which is based on sequence covariation, to have on average, weaker N-terminal anchor, RD-pocket, and C-terminal anchor interactions than STKs.
evidence: Inferred from Potts statistical energy analysis of residue-residue interactions

claim: The activation loop of TKs binds to the kinase's own active site as though it was engaging a peptide substrate in trans in the folded DFG-out conformation.
source: The remaining ~20% of the top contributions can be attributed to residue-residue interactions that occur within the folded DFG-out conformation wherein the activation loop of TKs binds to the kinase's own active site as though it was engaging a peptide substrate in trans (Figure 6C right) (Nolen et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nolen et al., 2004 and shown in Figure 6C

claim: STKs rarely adopt a folded DFG-out conformation with substrate-mimicking properties.
source: STKs, however, rarely adopt a folded DFG-out conformation with this property, and instead the activation loop is typically found to be unresolved and/or projecting outward toward solvent (Figure 6B right).
evidence: Based on structural observations shown in Figure 6B

claim: The substrate mimicry of the folded DFG-out activation loop observed in TKs is highly dependent on the presence of a Tyr phosphorylation site at position in the activation loop.
source: The Potts model suggests that this substrate mimicry of the folded DFG-out activation loop observed in TKs is highly dependent on the presence of a Tyr phosphorylation site at position in the activation loop (Figure 6C).
evidence: Inferred from Potts model analysis and shown in Figure 6C

claim: TK catalytic domains have a molecular evolutionary bias that shifts their conformational equilibrium toward the inactive 'folded activation loop' DFG-out state in the absence of activation signals.
source: To this end, we report evidence that TK catalytic domains have a molecular evolutionary bias that shifts their conformational equilibrium toward the inactive 'folded activation loop' DFG-out state in the absence of activation signals.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from combined Potts and ABFE simulation analyses

claim: STKs as a class have a more stable active conformation which is favored over the DFG-out state due to sequence constraints in the absence of other signals.
source: In contrast, STKs as a class have a more stable active conformation which is favored over the DFG-out state due to sequence constraints in the absence of other signals.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from combined Potts and ABFE simulation analyses

claim: The most potent type-II inhibitors from the literature which target STKs bind with nanomolar Kds, similar to that for TKs.
source: We note that the most potent type-II inhibitors from the literature which target STKs bind with nanomolar Kds, similar to that for TKs, despite the substantial additional reorganization penalty that STKs must overcome.
evidence: Based on literature-reported binding affinity data

claim: An MSA of 236,572 protein kinase catalytic domains with 259 columns was constructed.
source: An MSA of 236,572 protein kinase catalytic domains with 259 columns was constructed as previously described (McGee et al., 2021).
evidence: Methodological description with citation to McGee et al., 2021

claim: 10,345 raw sequences were classified as TKs (1069 effective sequences).
source: Kinases which satisfy the conditions for TKs at all three positions were classified as TKs (10,345 raw sequences, 1069 effective sequences), and those that satisfy the condition for STKs at position 126 and are non-overlapping with the TK condition at position 128 were classified as STKs (210,862 raw sequences, 22,893 effective sequences).
evidence: Methodological description of sequence classification

claim: 210,862 raw sequences were classified as STKs (22,893 effective sequences).
source: Kinases which satisfy the conditions for TKs at all three positions were classified as TKs (10,345 raw sequences, 1069 effective sequences), and those that satisfy the condition for STKs at position 126 and are non-overlapping with the TK condition at position 128 were classified as STKs (210,862 raw sequences, 22,893 effective sequences).
evidence: Methodological description of sequence classification

claim: 497 human kinase catalytic domain sequences were acquired from Modi and Dunbrack, 2019b.
source: 497 human kinase catalytic domain sequences were acquired from Modi and Dunbrack, 2019b (excluding atypical kinases).
evidence: Methodological description with citation

claim: 447 human kinases remained after filtering-out sequences with 32 or more gaps.
source: 447 human kinases remained after filtering-out sequences with 32 or more gaps.
evidence: Methodological description of data filtering

claim: Small gatekeepers have a volume of <110 Å³.
source: The designation of gatekeeper residues as 'large' or 'small' was based on sidechain van der Waals volumes (Miller et al., 1987; Figure 1—figure supplement 3), where small gatekeepers have a volume of <110 Å3 (Gly, Ala, Ser, Pro, Thr, Cys, Val), and large gatekeepers have a volume of >110 Å3 (Asn, His, Ile, Leu, Met, Lys, Phe, Glu, Tyr, Gln, Trp, Arg).
evidence: Methodological definition with citation to Miller et al., 1987

claim: Large gatekeepers have a volume of >110 Å³.
source: The designation of gatekeeper residues as 'large' or 'small' was based on sidechain van der Waals volumes (Miller et al., 1987; Figure 1—figure supplement 3), where small gatekeepers have a volume of <110 Å3 (Gly, Ala, Ser, Pro, Thr, Cys, Val), and large gatekeepers have a volume of >110 Å3 (Asn, His, Ile, Leu, Met, Lys, Phe, Glu, Tyr, Gln, Trp, Arg).
evidence: Methodological definition with citation to Miller et al., 1987

claim: 3643 structures in the BLAminus (active DFG-in) conformation belong to STKs and 625 structures belong to TKs (4268 structures in total).
source: Our analysis using the software provided in Modi and Dunbrack, 2019b identifies 3643 structures in this conformation belonging to STKs and 625 structures belonging to TKs (4268 structures in total).
evidence: Data from structural analysis using software from Modi and Dunbrack, 2019b

claim: 224 structures in the BBAminus (classical DFG-out) conformation belong to STKs and 286 structures belong to TKs (510 structures in total).
source: Our conformational analysis via Modi and Dunbrack, 2019b identifies 224 structures in this conformational state belonging to STKs and 286 structures belonging to TKs (510 structures in total).
evidence: Data from structural analysis using software from Modi and Dunbrack, 2019b

claim: A total of 94 different kinase-inhibitor complexes were simulated to calculate ABFEs via the alchemical DDM.
source: In this work, we have performed all-atom MD simulations in explicit solvent for a total of 94 different kinase-inhibitor complexes to calculate ABFEs via the alchemical DDM.
evidence: Methodological description of simulations performed

claim: 74 of the free-energy calculations were guided by insights from the Potts model.
source: 74 of these free-energy calculations were guided by insights from the Potts model, specifically the patterns of Potts conformational penalties plotted in Figure 1D.
evidence: Methodological description of simulation design

claim: TKs have properties which privilege the binding of type-II inhibitors in comparison to STKs.
source: As described below, our analysis of a previously published kinome-wide assay suggests that TKs have properties which privilege the binding of type-II inhibitors in comparison to STKs, which leads us to hypothesize an evolutionary divergence in their conformational energy landscapes.
evidence: Inferred from analysis of kinome-wide assay data

claim: TKs evolved to have free-energy penalties for the classical 'folded activation loop' DFG-out conformation relative to the active conformation that is, on average, 4–6 kcal/mol smaller than the corresponding values for STKs.
source: The structure-based and sequence-based analyses are consistent; together they suggest TKs evolved to have free-energy penalties for the classical 'folded activation loop' DFG-out conformation relative to the active conformation, that is, on average, 4–6 kcal/mol smaller than the corresponding values for STKs.
evidence: Conclusion from combined structure-based and sequence-based analyses

claim: The activation loops of TKs are more weakly 'anchored' against the catalytic loop motif in the active conformation.
source: Potts statistical energy analysis suggests a molecular basis for this observation, wherein the activation loops of TKs are more weakly 'anchored' against the catalytic loop motif in the active conformation and form more stable substrate-mimicking interactions in the inactive conformation.
evidence: Inferred from Potts statistical energy analysis

claim: The activation loops of TKs form more stable substrate-mimicking interactions in the inactive conformation.
source: Potts statistical energy analysis suggests a molecular basis for this observation, wherein the activation loops of TKs are more weakly 'anchored' against the catalytic loop motif in the active conformation and form more stable substrate-mimicking interactions in the inactive conformation.
evidence: Inferred from Potts statistical energy analysis
